title: SR 26-2: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management
pub: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
author: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System · Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation · Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The guidance reinforces selective, use-context-specific deployment and materially extends the cluster with a lifecycle model-risk framework: define intended purpose, involve expert users, scale testing and validation to materiality, monitor changing performance, and assign clear governance responsibilities. Although banking-focused rather than legal-specific, it strengthens the cluster’s governance and operating-model conclusions.
qs: Model risk can be mitigated through active and appropriate risk management, recognizing that  the relevance of model risk depends on the nature, scale, and use of the models in relation to the  associated business risks.
GOVERNANCE AND CONTROLS         All components of the model lifecycle benefit from model governance that is supported  by clear policies and effective controls.

st.t: Model assurance: Effective challenge needs institutional power
st.an: SR 26-2 directly supports lifecycle, risk-based governance and the cluster’s central claim that effective challenge requires expertise, objectivity and institutional influence. It also supports treating validation as qualified assurance rather than a safety guarantee. Its explicit exclusion of generative and agentic AI means it supports the legal-AI framework only by analogy, not as a directly applicable standard.
qs: Effective challenge is performed by individuals with the appropriate expertise to conduct a  critical and objective challenge, sufficient independence to maintain objectivity, as well as the  organizational standing and influence to effect any change.
Even with sound modeling practices and rigorous validation, material model risk can  remain.

kp.k: Guidance establishes nonbinding, risk-based banking model oversight
kp.d: The Federal Reserve, FDIC and OCC issue revised guidance based on supervisory experience, industry feedback and technological advancements. They recommend tailoring model risk management to each banking organization's model risk profile and operational size and complexity. These are supervisory recommendations rather than enforceable standards; the document nevertheless preserves supervisory action for violations of law or unsafe or unsound practices arising from insufficient model risk management.
qs: This guidance does not set forth enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements; accordingly, non-compliance with this guidance will not result in supervisory criticism against a banking organization.
However, supervisory action may result for any violations of law or unsafe or unsound practices stemming from insufficient management of model risk.

kp.k: Asset threshold qualifies the guidance's intended relevance
kp.d: The guidance is expected to be most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 billion in total assets. Organizations at or below $30 billion are generally excluded in favor of size- and risk-appropriate internal governance, but the guidance may remain relevant where model prevalence, complexity or activities outside traditional community banking create significant model risk.
qs: This guidance is expected to be most relevant to banking organizations with over $30
billion in total assets.
However, in some situations, this guidance also may be relevant to banking organizations with total assets of $30 billion or less

kp.k: Generative and agentic AI are explicitly outside scope
kp.d: The agencies exclude generative and agentic AI because these models are novel and rapidly evolving. They nevertheless recommend that organizational risk management and governance guide controls for excluded systems. The principles apply to traditional statistical and quantitative models and non-generative, non-agentic AI, not to all AI indiscriminately.
qs: Generative AI and agentic AI models are novel and rapidly evolving. As such, they are not within the scope of this guidance.

Nonetheless, a banking organization’s risk management and governance practices should guide the determination of appropriate governance and controls for any tools, processes, or systems not covered in this document.
However, the principles described in this guidance apply to traditional statistical and quantitative models and non-generative, non-agentic AI models.

kp.k: Model definition excludes simple calculations and rule-based software
kp.d: The document defines models as complex quantitative approaches applying statistical, economic or financial theories to turn input data into quantitative estimates. Simple spreadsheet arithmetic and deterministic processes or software lacking those theoretical foundations are excluded.
qs: For the purposes of this guidance, the term “model” refers to a complex quantitative
method, system, or approach that applies statistical, economic, or financial theories to process
input data into quantitative estimates.

kp.k: Model benefits coexist with potentially substantial financial risks
kp.d: The agencies describe growing model complexity and scope, driven by technology and competition, and regard continued model use as essential to banking competitiveness. They identify potential financial losses, reporting errors and flawed financial or risk management decisions as associated risks. These are institutional assessments, not quantified empirical findings.
qs: Continued use of models is essential to maintaining the competitiveness of banking organizations in the financial system.
Use of models also can present substantial risk.

kp.k: Materiality determines proportionate oversight alongside inherent risk
kp.d: Inherent risk reflects assumptions, complexity, input quality and data constraints. Exposure concerns the significance of outputs to business decisions; purpose concerns the nature and importance of use. Exposure and purpose jointly determine materiality. Models supporting regulatory requirements or financial risk management are generally considered higher risk; immaterial models may receive identification and monitoring rather than comprehensive oversight.
qs: Model purpose, together with model exposure, determines model materiality.
Assessing
risk based on model materiality is an important consideration for sound model risk management.

kp.k: Misuse and shared dependencies create additional model risks
kp.d: The guidance distinguishes model soundness from safe application: even accurate models may pose high risk when misapplied. It recommends assessing both individual and aggregate risk, including dependencies and common assumptions, data or methodologies capable of affecting multiple models simultaneously.
qs: However, even a fundamentally sound
model producing accurate outputs consistent with the model’s design objective can exhibit high
model risk if it is misapplied or misused.
Sound practice involves assessing model risk both individually and in aggregate.

kp.k: Effective challenge requires expertise, independence and organizational influence
kp.d: The agencies define effective challenge as objective expert scrutiny capable of producing changes throughout the model lifecycle. Its effectiveness depends not just on technical expertise but also on sufficient independence and organizational standing to secure changes.
qs: Effective challenge is performed by individuals with the appropriate expertise to conduct a
critical and objective challenge, sufficient independence to maintain objectivity, as well as the
organizational standing and influence to effect any change.

kp.k: Development combines technical testing, judgment and user input
kp.d: The guidance treats model development as multidisciplinary and judgment-dependent rather than purely technical. It recommends a clear statement of purpose, engagement with users and business managers, and testing tailored to complexity and materiality. Suggested tests include out-of-sample and out-of-time testing, alternative assumptions or methodologies, and assessment of data quality and relevance.
qs: Model development is not purely a technical exercise.
Input from model users can enhance model development by providing business context
and practical insights.
The rigor of effective testing is commensurate with model complexity and
materiality.

kp.k: Extending model use introduces uncertainty and warrants reassessment
kp.d: Effective use requires understanding limitations and assessing performance as conditions change. When a model is applied beyond its original purpose, the agencies recommend considering additional analysis of the new use and reviewing existing controls to address the resulting risk.
qs: Using a model beyond its intended purpose introduces additional uncertainty and risk.
When extending a model’s use beyond its original application, sound practice involves
considering additional analysis of the new usage and its limitations, along with review of
existing controls to manage the resulting risk.

kp.k: Validation timing and rigor depend on model circumstances
kp.d: Validation assesses expected performance, reliability and limitations, with timing and rigor varying by purpose, methodology, changes and practical constraints. It generally precedes first use, but urgent business need may justify earlier deployment with attention to limitations, stakeholder communication and controls such as usage limits or closer monitoring. Validation quality depends on review effectiveness rather than organizational structure.
qs: Validation generally occurs prior to a model’s first use.
However, certain circumstances (e.g., an urgent business need) may necessitate using the model
before validation is completed.
The quality of validation process depends on the rigor and effectiveness of the review
rather than on organizational structure of the banking organization’s risk management function.

kp.k: Validation examines conceptual soundness and real-world outcomes
kp.d: Conceptual validation assesses model design, assumptions, judgments, data selection, construction and developmental testing. Interpretability measures or benchmarking may be more practical than theoretical assessment for some models. Outcomes analysis compares outputs with real-world outcomes; material errors or persistent deviations may warrant adjustment, recalibration or redevelopment. Quantitative analysis can also assess models that rely heavily on expert judgment.
qs: Outcomes analysis compares model outputs to corresponding real-world outcomes to
assess model performance relative to model objectives and business use.
When a model’s
design relies substantially on expert judgment, quantitative outcomes analysis helps to evaluate
the quality of that judgment.

kp.k: Monitoring addresses deterioration without eliminating residual risk
kp.d: The agencies caution that sound modeling and rigorous validation can leave material risk. They recommend communicating limitations, reviewing continued relevance and supplementing outputs with other information. Monitoring should assess changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance and markets; deterioration may warrant overlays, adjustment or redevelopment. Monitoring frequency and scope depend on model characteristics, new data or methods, and materiality.
qs: Even with sound modeling practices and rigorous validation, material model risk can
remain.
A model that no longer performs as expected may warrant
overlays, adjustment, or redevelopment of the model depending on a banking organization’s model risk management policy as it pertains to model deterioration.

kp.k: Governance clarifies accountability without duplicating operational model work
kp.d: The guidance recommends clear policies, controls and lifecycle responsibilities, including management of conflicts between development and validation incentives. Where internal audit participates, its role generally concerns the effectiveness of risk management and policy implementation rather than repeating development or validation. External resources require organizational oversight and integration. Inventories support individual and aggregate risk understanding, while documentation supports continuity, tracking and remediation.
qs: Model risk management benefits from clear roles and responsibilities with well-defined
accountability, including with respect to potential conflicts of interest
internal audit would generally not duplicate model risk management activities such as model
development or validation.
Adequate documentation helps to support effective model risk management.

kp.k: Vendor opacity does not displace model risk management
kp.d: Proprietary vendor models, data and parameters can restrict access to underlying code, data or methods and complicate validation. The agencies nevertheless recommend validation by internal or outside parties, understanding model design and performance, and ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis. Customizations should be documented, justified and evaluated during validation.
qs: Nevertheless, the
principles of model risk management remain applicable.
An important element of model risk management is the validation of vendor products,
either by internal or outside parties.
In cases
where vendor models are customized to fit a banking organization’s specific business needs, sound practice also involves appropriately documenting, justifying, and evaluating adjustments
made to customize the model as part of model validation.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The agencies address banking model risk, not legal services: non-generative, non-agentic AI falls within the guidance, while generative and agentic AI is expressly excluded.
pts.d: The Federal Reserve Board, FDIC and OCC describe growing model complexity and scope, and associate innovative modeling approaches with efficiency, risk mitigation and profitability. These are broad claims about banking models rather than measured AI-specific effects. They also state that model use can cause financial losses, reporting errors and flawed decisions. Their concrete AI-specific position is that traditional model-risk principles apply to non-generative, non-agentic AI, whereas rapidly evolving generative and agentic AI requires governance determined through the bank’s broader risk-management practices. The source does not predict lawyer displacement, legal-service market changes or quantified AI productivity gains.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The stated basis is supervisory experience, industry feedback and technological developments, rather than empirical AI performance evidence.
pts.d: The agencies present supervisory principles grounded in their experience and industry input. They do not supply datasets, quantitative benchmarks, named incidents or measured AI adoption or productivity outcomes. Validation, outcomes analysis and ongoing monitoring are recommended methods for banks to assess their own models; they are not reported research findings supporting a quantified claim about AI’s effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The April 17, 2026 guidance states current supervisory principles, with no forecast horizon; application depends on model type, materiality and institutional risk.
pts.d: The generative and agentic AI exclusion is framed in terms of their current novelty and rapid evolution, without specifying when that exclusion might change. The guidance is expected to be most relevant to banks above $30 billion in assets, with possible relevance to smaller banks that have significant model-risk exposure. Oversight is to be proportionate to model complexity, materiality and use. Validation generally precedes first use, but urgent business needs may justify earlier use accompanied by attention to limitations and appropriate controls. The guidance itself is not enforceable, although violations of law or unsafe or unsound practices arising from insufficient model-risk management may lead to supervisory action.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected parties are banking organizations, model developers, users, validators, governance personnel and third-party model providers.
pts.d: Banks retain responsibility for model-risk practices suited to their own risks, including governance for tools excluded from this document. Developers and users contribute technical and business judgments; objective experts provide effective challenge; validation and monitoring assess reliability and limitations. Where internal audit participates, its role is generally to assess the effectiveness of model-risk management rather than duplicate development or validation. Vendor products can create additional assessment difficulties because proprietary components may limit access to underlying information, but the agencies maintain that model-risk principles still apply. These are banking governance implications, not claims about changes to legal occupations or legal-service providers.
